doc.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998

title: Playing overseas and the economics of touring with pick-up bands
summary: Response abroad is less special now; American musicians play small pubs, European audiences have continuity, and Bob prefers a formed group to jam sessions.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Yeah. We had an earlier conversation about the importance placed on jazz in this country and abroad. Does it make a difference when you go overseas to play, in the response?

Yes it does. Less than it used to, because I think that now it’s become commonplace. American musicians are appearing on the doorstep just about every other day. And it’s been known for certain musicians from the United States to appear twice in our little country in England. And they are not necessarily filling halls, they’re working in small

pubs and places like that. It’s beneath them, beneath their talent, and I don’t approve of them having to do that. But unfortunately it’s the only way. If you want to do two tours a year you can’t do them both in concert halls you see? I think that now the message has gotten out, and certainly some of the Swedish are brilliant players. Bob’s student Antti Sarpila from Finland has a band and is playing all the time. Antti is a phenomenally talented musician. I think that it’s taking the edge off the American standard of playing. First of all you have to realize the attrition rate among the legends, in quote legends of jazz, has been very hard on us all, and we’ve lost so many fine players. And there hasn’t been a continuum. The musicians have not been sort of growing up and following in their footsteps and staying with it as Bob has for instance and a number of other people who have been enamored of the music. So there has been a dearth of players to fill those shoes so that now you can go to England and the musicians are picking up with a pianist and a rhythm section so they don’t have to take over a rhythm section. I think that there’s a great love of the music that’s different in other countries, and I think that people are always willing to pay the dues to the United States for having created, being that it has spawned this music. And I think they’re delighted that young Johnny is playing along with the jazz records and will no doubt join the school jazz bands, however it sounds. And there are jazz programs starting throughout the United Kingdom, probably in the same way that they are in this country. In Switzerland for instance, there’s a great tradition of jazz. For instance when Hans Weber, who is a dear friend and a promoter of jazz, has a jazz festival in May in Berne, you play one day at The Rathskeller, where there are people bringing their babies and these people were brought there by their parents. Now that is exciting, because their parents are familiar with all the musicians they’re going to see play, and their children are familiar with it. That’s wonderful.
You’ve got some continuity there, it’s really establishing it.

Yes, absolutely. And the same thing applies in other places in England for instance, when people have some frame of reference for what they have seen and they continue to watch and so on. But I think the economics of bringing over musicians is getting harder, and one of the problems that we have, Bobby and I subscribe to as well, is that Bob doesn’t like jam sessions. He really likes a formed group, because as you notice from our recordings, we like musicians that have at least shook hands before they go on the stage. They should at least have practiced a couple of things together. And it gets harder, because these musicians are being asked would you like to come over and do two weeks in England or Germany or somewhere, and you arrive at the airport and you’re picked up by the promoter and you meet all the musicians and this is Fred and this Jack and this, and so on, and you make whatever music you can make.
